articles.text: The state of California has been expanding a Transitional Kindergarten (TK) program since 2022 and which will add an extra grade of school for four year olds by 2025. Architect Ector Mojica from Quattrocchi Kwok Architects (QKA) advised Piedmont’s School Board of its options to accommodate the new students during an August 14 school board meeting. There are 79 students in four TK classes in Piedmont this year; students that turned four by June 2 were eligible. Next year the eligibility will open up to any kids that turn four by September 1. For the 2025–26 school year, the District anticipates needing at least one more classroom to accommodate the new students. “Our administrators see kids coming and they don’t know where we are going to put them,” explained PUSD CBO Ruth Alahydoian. Mojica showed the board three options (A,B, & C) for each site. Potential facility changes included low-cost ways (option As) to shuffle classroom assignments around. At Havens the option A was to put a TK class in room 117 and migrate classrooms to keep grades together. Some options create TK and K combo classes, and some options involve some construction. The architect went over specific changes at each site, including one that would remove the Wildwood Schoolmates portable and build a new learning space. Mojica and board member Hilary Cooper talked about avoiding critique from the Division of the State Architect’s (DSA) office. Traditionally, Labor Day is the starting point for the most intense political awareness and involvement. Thus, I offer a few thoughts as we prepare to vote. 1. The right to vote must not be disrespected or neglected. In the long history of humanity, the right to vote for our leaders, laws and policies is a relatively new, hard-earned and very vulnerable right. Many of our foremothers and forefathers made great sacrifices in order that their children and grandchildren could vote. For that we praise them. Yet, praising them without thoughtfully exercising the right to vote is meaningless. 2. Our votes should be a reflection of our values. While we do not all share the same values, it is incumbent on each of us to vote in a way that expresses our goals for our communities, our vision for our country and our hopes for our world. Most of us would say that the well-being of the next generations is a high value for us. I would urge us to vote accordingly. 3. Freedom of conscience matters. One reason that faith leaders should, refrain from, or at least be very cautious about instructing their communities how to vote is our belief that freedom of conscience always matters and that, like voting, it is a sacred right. 4. Self-interest matters. It would be naïve to suggest that our own well-being should not matter when it comes to casting our ballots. However, self-interest need not be narrow or selfish. I firmly believe that there is such a thing as enlightened self-interest, the understanding that when you thrive, it is much more likely that I will thrive, the belief that when you are better-off, it is much more likely that I will be better off. 5. articles.text: As a child, Lucas Romero’s parents took him for a tour of his local fire station. He remembers fondly the way he marched through the halls, took pictures of riding on the fire engine and pretended to spray a hose on imaginary fires around him. It’s a memory that he considers dear, especially now that he’s the one giving the tours. “I would say it’s come full circle,” he laughed. Firefighter Paramedic Lucas Romero, 27, is one of the newest recruits to the Piedmont Fire Department. Hired in January 2024, Romero brings with him experience as an EMT in San Joaquin County. He also brings a cheerful personality which has allowed him to mesh well with the other members of the department. Lucas Romero was born in 1997 in Tracy, and soon after his birth his family moved to Manteca. He attended Neil Hafley Elementary School and then graduated from East Union High School in 2015. After graduation, Romero briefly attended Delta College in Stockton before deciding that a career in academia wasn’t the best fit. In 2018, Romero decided he wanted to change careers. “I was climbing a pole for my job, and it was pouring rain. I saw an ambulance drive by with its lights flashing, and I remember thinking how cool that job would be,” recalled Romero. “That’s Lucas Romero was pinned by his girlfriend Kylee Killion at a Piedmont City Council meeting on July 15. Staff Photos Firefighter Paramedic Lucas Romero, hired in January, recently completed his Fire Academy training and was pinned with a Piedmont Fire Dept. badge at City Hall on July 15. when I decided to dive head-first into being a first responder.” Only a few weeks later, a position opened at his local fire department, and Romero applied immediately. “Fate has a funny way of working like that,” he laughed. That same year, Romero began working part-time as a reserve with the Manteca Fire Department and earned an EMT license from Abrams College in Modesto. In 2020, he joined American Medical Response in San Joaquin County as an EMT, where he worked a busy schedule encompassing several cities. “We covered Stockton, Lodi, Tracy, and many others,” he explained. “It was good experience, especially for what I do now.” Romero heard about the Piedmont Fire Department and after taking a written exam for the Firefighter Candidate Testing Center, Romero met Piedmont Fire Lieutenant Brian Gidney, who was handing out job flyers at the testing site. Romero applied in September 2023 and was given a conditional offer by the end of the month. Romero’s first impressions of Piedmont were like “a breath of fresh air,” and he said that the city has been extremely welcoming. “Some cities, they don’t care for their fire department, and some fire departments don’t care for their new hires. That’s not the case here.” Additionally, Romero said that the Piedmont Fire Department is different than any job he has had in the past, especially concerning its morale and quality of service. “You’ve got guys who take firefighting seriously. Captain Fitzpatrick’s huge on working out. We have a mandatory 90-minute workout every day. In Piedmont, you have to be ready for the job and do it well. And it’s all for the citizens,” he said. Romero was officially hired by the department in January, and on Monday, July 15, after five months of training at Las Positas College’s East Bay Regional Fire Academy in Livermore, Romero was sworn in at City Hall during a regularly scheduled City Council meeting. articles.text: Message to community from former School Board candidate Victoria Rosenbaum: Thank you to all my supporters who encouraged me to run for a PUSD Board seat in the upcoming election. I have a great interest in the continued excellence of PUSD, and as an educator, parent, and resident of this wonderful city, I know that I would add an important perspective to the issues facing our schools. However, after much consideration, I have decided that this is not the right time for me to serve on the PUSD School Board. Unfortunately, I have been informed by the City Clerk that it is not possible to remove my name from the ballot. In light of that fact, I am endorsing the candidacies of Susy Struble, Michael Malione and Max Roman and am encouraging others to support them, too. They each have unique strengths, perspectives, and a strong desire to promote PUSD’s mission, and I believe PUSD will continue to thrive with them at the helm. articles.text: Life is filled with transitions, whether we like it or not. From childhood to adulthood, starting a new job, or even moving to a new city, transitions happen to all of us. And let’s be honest—they’re rarely easy. It doesn’t matter how old you are or what stage of life you’re in; change brings uncertainty, and uncertainty often brings stress. But if there’s one thing we know for sure, it’s that transitions are inevitable. For some, transitions come a little easier. But for most of us, change can feel overwhelming. What if, instead of dreading transitions, we embraced them as opportunities? What if we saw transitions not as disruptions, but as invitations to grow? The key to navigating transitions with ease lies in adopting a creative mindset—a way of thinking that transforms the way we approach change. Embrace the creative mindset The creative mindset is about seeing the world through a lens of possibilities. When we shift our perspective, transitions stop seeming so scary. Instead of focusing on the fear of the unknown, we start to recognize the exciting potential that comes with change. It’s the difference between saying, “This is going to be hard,” and asking, “What can I learn from this?” One of the most powerful aspects of a creative mindset is that it allows us to anticipate transitions. Rather than being blindsided, we can recognize when changes are on the horizon and prepare ourselves to ride the wave. Instead of resisting, we can embrace the shift, knowing we have the tools to navigate it. How to foster a creative mindset If the creative mindset is the key to making transitions smoother, how do we cultivate it? One of the most effective ways is by learning to view the world as malleable—not fixed or binary. Life is rarely a matter of “right” or “wrong”; it’s filled with nuance and complexity. To practice this kind of thinking, start with small, low-stakes decisions. Let’s say you’re deciding what to have for dinner. Instead of defaulting to your usual pizza or Thai, make a list of all the possibilities. Could you try a new recipe? Explore a different cuisine? The goal here isn’t necessarily to pick the perfect option but to open yourself up to variety. Another exercise is to seek out ways that your perspective can be both right and wrong at the same time. This is not about doubting yourself but about exploring multiple dimensions to every situation. When you do this, you build mental flexibility, which makes it easier to handle transitions because you become more comfortable with uncertainty and open to new solutions. Navigating change with confidence Transitions are never easy, but they don’t have to be paralyzing. we can reframe the way we see change—from something to fear to something full of possibilities. The next time you find yourself on the brink of a transition, whether big or small, try leaning into the creative process. You’ll find that when you start thinking in terms of possibility, change becomes less of a wave to fear and more of an adventure to embrace. T is for Transition, but it’s also for Transformation. Nina Meehan is a Speaker, Consultant and Workshop Leader with a specialization in the 3Cs: Creativity, Communication and Connection. https://ninameehan. com/

To practice this kind of thinking, start with small, low-stakes decisions. Let’s say you’re deciding what to have for dinner. Instead of defaulting to your usual pizza or Thai, make a list of all the possibilities. Could you try a new recipe? Explore a different cuisine? The goal here isn’t necessarily to pick the perfect option but to open yourself up to variety. Another exercise is to seek out ways that your perspective can be both right and wrong at the same time. This is not about doubting yourself but about exploring multiple dimensions to every situation. When you do this, you build mental flexibility, which makes it easier to handle transitions because you become more comfortable with uncertainty and open to new solutions. Navigating change with confidence Transitions are never easy, but they don’t have to be paralyzing. By nurturing a creative mindset, we can reframe the way we see change—from something to fear to something full of possibilities. The next time you find yourself on the brink of a transition, whether big or small, try leaning into the creative process. You’ll find that when you start thinking in terms of possibility, change becomes less of a wave to fear and more of an adventure to embrace. T is for Transition, but it’s also for Transformation. Some groups make their squares a family affair. Raul Jorcino, co-founder of the Chalk Art Festival, re-created a drawing from the popular children’s book Goodnight Moon (1947) with the help of his son Tómas, 18. The duo divided their chalk square into a series of grids and faithfully re-drew the scene piece by piece to make sure every detail was included. “I think every kid will recognize the art here because many like to read this book at night. It’s a classic,” said Raul Jorcino. All the while, children ran around the perimeter of the squares, shouting and playing games. The mood was upbeat and convivial, and many artists took time to walk around and appreciate one another’s work when they were finished. As is custom, the chalk art drawings will remain on the blacktop until they fade away naturally or are washed away by rain. In the meantime, they will serve as a colorful addition to the school for Beach kids to run by, play on and admire for weeks to come. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont High School boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan resigned earlier this summer. He is one of the most successful soccer coaches in school history. He is shown after his team won the 2022 North Coast Section championship. During the summer, Piedmont High boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan, originally from England, announced a big change in his life. He has elected to step away from coaching the high school game. Still coaching at the club level at 24-7 UK Soccer Academy, Sullivan decided he wanted to spend more time with one-year old son. After eight years at the school, Sullivan becomes one of Piedmont’s most successful soccer coach in school history. “It was a tough decision,” he said. “With the family, the plan was to get back to the UK before the 2024 season and I wouldn’t be able to coach. But, for now, we’re staying in the U.S. Hopefully now I’ll be able to catch some games without being a coach. It was a great eight years. There was never a season where we didn’t give it everything as a school,” Sullivan said. Sullivan revived Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer program, achieving several honors. His teams finished on top of the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division in 2019, 2021, and 2022, earning the a promotion to the Foothill Division. But his greatest accomplishment was leading the team to back-to-back Division 4 North Coast Section titles in 2022 and 2023. The first title came in a 1-0 win over No. 2 University as the No. 1 seed at Witter Field. The second was another 1-nil win over No. 2 University, this time coming as the tournament’s Cinderella story as a No. 8 seed. Piedmont now plays in Division 3 after a promotion in 2023. The 2022 NCS title was the boys’ team’s s first section title in school history. The second NCS championship was a surprise. Piedmont was the No. 8 seed that year. “I’ve been asked this a few times and I always answer the same – one title isn’t more special than the other. We had fantastic players the first year we won it, then were underdogs the next year against some really good teams. The boys really did take the mantra of having a tough, hardworking identity. “The 2023 team if anything was more surprising to people on our team and perhaps the larger soccer world in the Bay Area. People recognized Piedmont as a serious team. I’d go as far to say the 2023 probably had a greater impact on the school.” 2019 marked the school’s first league championship in 10 years. That February night when Piedmont claimed the WACC banner appeared to be the turning point of the program. Sullivan signed on as head coach in the winter of 2016-17, replacing Rory O’Connor. In four years as head coach, O’Conner had one NCS win and finished with a positive winning percentage just one time. PHS went 9-2-9 (W-T-L) in Sullivan’s first year and 7-2-13 in his second year when still developing a system change – Todd Sullivan concludes his time at Piedmont with 87 wins and 155 total matches as head coach.

Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team continues pushing through its difficult pre-league schedule looking for its first victory of the season. They suffered a 3-1 loss to Skyline on the road in Oakland on Wednesday, September 4, lost 3-0 at Campolindo in Moraga the next day, and lost 3-1 to San Rafael at home in Binks Rawlings Gym on Monday, September 9. Final stats for the losses to Campolindo and San Rafael were not provided. “We just haven’t done well with adversity. We seemed timid being in a gym that’s hot like Skyline’s and a crowd that’s aggressive. I’ll be saying this all season long, but we’re young and we need to grow into ourselves before we start being really successful,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. Against Skyline, Piedmont won the second set 25-15 to tie the match at 1-1. However, PHS couldn’t execute at the same consistency in the final two sets of the match, falling 25-18, 25-16 to close. “We couldn’t get under the short-serves. If our errors outweigh our successes, of course we’re going to lose. But you can see glimpses of success, it’s finding a way to maintain that when we have it going,” Cardenas said. articles.text: Piedmont’s JV football team suffered its first loss of the season on Friday, September 6 at Witter Field, falling 27-14 to the visiting Middletown Mustangs after committing four turnovers on the afternoon. PHS tied Salesian the previous week in its season-opener. This week’s captains were sophomore Henry Brennan, and freshmen Jimmy Lagios, Joaquin Fierro, and George Saunders. Brennan was called up to varsity last week against Salesian. The Highlanders received the opening kickoff but threw an interception on the third play of the game. Middletown drove toward the goal line, and although the PHS’ defense got three straight stops inside the five-yard line, the Mustangs punched the ball across on the fourth down. Piedmont’s offense came out looking to change the momentum. Starting at their own 45 yard line, Lagios tossed a screen pass to receiver Diego Hurwitz on the first play, taking it 55yards to the end zone for a 7-7 tie. After multiple trades of possession, Piedmont defensive back Owen Curran intercepted a Mustangs pass on a deep pass down the sideline. Unfortunately, the Highlanders couldn’t capitalize and both sides went into halftime knotted up at 7-7. Middletown opened with possession in the third quarter, but Piedmont’s defense forced a punt. On the ensuing possession, Lagios and Hurwitz connected for another big play to get the Highlanders into the red zone. Hurwitz then scored on an endaround for his second touchdown of the game, putting PHS up 14-7. However, the Highlanders’ joy was short-lived after the Mustangs answered with a touchdown of their own on the next possession. But on the ensuing kickoff Piedmont relinquishing a crucial fumble to Middletown, giving them great field position. The Mustangs ran the ball through the Highlander defense to score a go-ahead touchdown, 21-14. On the Highlanders’ next possession, Middletown nabbed an interception to take it all the way to the end zone increasing the deficit to 27-14 with two minutes to go. The Highlanders look to bounce back this Friday against Mt. Eden of Hayward. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-1-1) hosts Mt. Eden on Friday, September 13 for a 4:00 p.m. game. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse launches its 2024-25 season with The Prom, performing now through Sunday, October 13. The Prom is a musical telling the story of four Broadway actors and actresses who visit a small town in Indiana to champion a local high school student’s right to bring her girlfriend to the prom. The play, based on a book by Bob Martin, was originally performed on Broadway in 2018 and was later made into a movie featuring Meryl Streep and Nicole Kidman. The Berkeley Playhouse production is co-directed and co-choreographed by Megan McGrath and Christina Lazo, with music directed by Daniel Alley. Berkeley Playhouse Artistic Director Kimberly Dooley said she was thrilled to select The Prom as the theater’s celebratory season opener. “This musical is bursting with so much heart and humor, plus it’s full of laughter and fantastic dancing,” said Dooley. “It’s the perfect show to open our new season for its messages of acceptance, joy, friendship and love for all.” “There have been instances over the years across the country of parents pulling their students from high school productions and local theaters canceling their shows due to the material,” said co-director Christina Lazo. “So we have to keep doing shows like this. I can’t wait for audiences to see the sparkle and the beauty of the world within The Prom.” The play features Arri Toshiko Glenn as Emma Nolan, Aleshani Altan as Alyssa Greene, Taylor Bartolucci as Dee Dee Allen, DC Scarpelli as Barry Glickman and Mary Kalita as Angie Dickenson. To purchase to tickets and see showtimes, visit https://tickets. berkeleyplayhouse.org/
articles.title: The Prom at Berkeley Playhouse through Oct. 13

articles.text: The de Young Museum, one of the fine arts museums in San Francisco, is exhibiting impressionist and realist artworks spanning the period of 1848 to 1960 in an exhibition entitled American Beauty now through October 20. American art in the 19th and 20th centuries presents a variety of artistic responses during a complex period in US history. Artwork featured is borrowed from the collection of Bernard and Barbro Osher, which enhances the de Young’s American art collection with several significant firsts. The exhibition includes the first large-scale oil painting by Winslow Homer (The Angler, ca. 1874), the first genre picture by William Merritt Chase (Spanish Bric-à-Brac Shop, 1883), the first major George Bellows landscape (In Virginia, 1908), the first Georgia O’Keeffe images of the Southwest (Front of Ranchos Church, 1930 and The Patio, 1940), as well as 13 artists on display at the museum for the first time. To learn more about the exhibition and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.famsf.org/exhibitions/osher-american-art. The American Beauty exhibition will be on view at the de Young through October.
articles.title: De Young Museum hosts American Beauty exhibition

articles.text: AXIS Dance Company, an acclaimed ensemble of disabled and neurodiverse dancers, will perform Friday-Sunday, October 11-13, at San Francisco’s ODC Theater. A Bay Area-based dance company, Axis was founded in 1987 and has toured over 100 cities in the U.S., the United Kingdom, Europe and the United Arab Emirates. AXIS’s mission is to create world-class productions that challenge perceptions and redefine dance and disability. Next month AXIS will perform new choreography for its home season Ecos, with Berkeley-based contemporary dance company “Post:ballet” serving as special guests. “Ecos brings together extraordinary artists to explore the complexities of our shared human experience,” said AXIS Dance Company’s Artistic Director Nadia Adame. “Each piece in this Home Season reflects a unique perspective, yet together they resonate with a powerful, collective spirit. This season is a heartfelt invitation to connect, reflect, and be moved together.” Tickets for Ecos are available now at www.axisdance.org. AXIS Dance Company artists perform onstage. articles.text: A scene from Pirate Radio On any given Friday or Saturday night in the 1950s and early 1960s, it was not unusual to pull into a drive-in restaurant filled with cars and kids, some leaning against fenders, others deep in conversation, and hear on more than one car radio Wolfman Jack, a rock & roll DJ legend. “Let’s git nakkid” he’d call out as he segued into “It’s All Right (Mama)” by Elvis Presley, one of the first and perhaps greatest rock & roll songs ever. Wolfman Jack with his signature gravelly voice and a diabolical laugh. No one had ever seen him. He was an enigma. Rumor had it that he was on some ship off the coast of Mexico, staying one record spin ahead of the culture cops. Or possibly he was holed up in a beachside, cinderblock shack with a monster antenna, south of Tijuana. And, as it turned out, that’s exactly where the Wolfman was, in Mexico, slammin’ and jammin’ at station XERB-AM, sending out a powerhouse signal to all places north, up the coast of California, even reaching Alaska on a clear night. What was undisputed was that the discs Wolfman played captured the essence of being young during the late 50s and early 60s. Rock & roll was transcendent. It was heart wrenching, spine-tingling, drop to your knees wonderful. And more. There was Big Joe Turner’s Shake, Rattle & Roll and Bill Haley and the Comet’s Rock Around the Clock, all precursors of some of the most vital, Motown inspired music to ever come out of the 50s, soon morphing into the Stones, Buddy Holly, Chuck Berry, Fats Domino, James Brown and the Beach Boys. Rock & roll was the cresting wave, a cultural zeitgeist. It defined a generation. Great Britain, in so many ways, mirrored America, creating its own unique version of rock & roll, led by groups such as The Who, The Kinks, Cream, Pink Floyd and, of course, The Beatles. And for a time, in the 60s, British kids tuned in late at night to a rogue rock & roll station, beamed from a ship somewhere off the coast. And that is the essence of the film, Pirate Radio. An improbable group of disc jockeys who kept rock & roll on the radio 24/7, to the absolute delight of the nation’s listeners and to the consternation of the British government and the BBC, which took great umbrage at the airways being filled with such “rot.” Led by Cultural Minister Alistair Dormandy (Kenneth Brannagh), a concerted effort is set in motion to sink the renegade ship, so to speak, and shut down the illicit music once and for all. Rock & roll, it was decided, posed a threat to homeland security. Meanwhile, on board, the DJs are running a floating animal house, engaging in pranks and fun and music. The housemother, so to speak, is Quentin (Bill Nighy), the captain and titular head of this ragged crew, with The Count (Philip Seymour Hoffman) and Gavin (Rhys Ifans) filling the prime time radio slots. While the story is thin – there is a subplot, a sort of coming-ofage saga about young Carl, the nephew of Quentin – the energy and sheer delight conveyed by the film makes for sweet entertainment and the sound track, meaning the platters spun, is, simply, top drawer. Pirate Radio. Starring Philip Seymour Hoffman, Bill Nighy, Rhys Ifans, Talulah Riley and Tom Sturridge. Directed by Richard Curtis. 2 hrs., 9 min. Rated R. Released in 2009. Banning, after years of getting banged up is now stoically suffering from a compressed vertebrae and serious aches and pains plus a growing addiction to painkillers. articles.text: Castle in the Sky is a swashbuckling, Indiana Jones steampunk adventure that also manages to weave into its narrative a subtle ecological message. But above all it’s for kids. From the get-go, the story is gripping and in the first opening scenes there’s a kidnapping attempt of a young orphan girl Sheeta (Anna Paquin) by a secret, nefarious agent called Muska (Mark Hamil). She is flown via airship to a military fortress, but on the way the ship is attacked by a cohort of air pirates, all led by captain Dola (Cloris Leachman). The reason for the raid is to steal a precious, mysterious amulet that Sheeta wears around her neck, a gift to her from her grandmother. During the attack, Sheeta falls from the ship and instead of crashing to earth she floats gently down into the arms of a dreamy teenage boy, Pazu (James Van Der Beek). Together they set out on a hold your breath, hide from the pirates adventure, a quest that leads them to a floating mythical, steampunk island called Laputa that hovers just above earth. Its source of power is a crystal, not unlike Sheeta’s amulet. Sheeta and Pazu are scrappy, courageous protagonists who relish getting into and out of sequential jams. The story is fast-paced and while there is gunplay, and the bad guys and designated villains bite the dirt, so to speak, Miyazaki is never relies on graA scene from Studio Ghibli’s Castle in the Sky tuitous, wham-bang, shots-fired action drama. It’s all in service of a let’er rip story. Castle in the Sky is no exception. It’s pure fun fantasy. The artwork is hand-drawn (part of Ghibli’s brand) and astonishingly good (in many ways richer than those works created by CGI) depicting some wonderful chase scenes featuring a train racing across a wobbly trellis, dogfights between massive airplanes and shoot-outs between floating dirigibles and war ships. Meanwhile, as Sheeta and Pazu discover, Laputa is a remarkable medieval place, with crumbling castles, overrun with weeds and vines, marginally maintained by a crew of robots. Underground they discover that the technology that keeps Laputa afloat is not dissimilar from Sheeta’s magical amulet. If you have not introduced your youngsters to the amazing work of Studio Ghibli and the extraordinary art and storytelling of Mayao Miyazaki, Castle in the Sky is a fine beginning. Castle in the Sky. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Animé fantasy from Studio Ghibli. With voices of James Van Der Beek, Anna Paquin, Cloris Leachman, Mark Hamil and Mandy Patinkin. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG. Released in 2019, Now streaming on Fandango/prime/ MAX.

articles.text: Before discussing the latest entry to the Marvel Comics Universe (MCU), I pause to make full disclosure. When I was a kid my favorite superhero was, indeed, Captain Marvel. As drawn and written in Marvel comics the Captain was a guy. He had the physique of Superman with an orange cape, matching tights with a lightning bolt in the center of his chest. Very cool. He possessed, like Batman and Superman, superhuman abilities. I recall that my mom sewed an orange cape for me with silver piping at the edges. It sat perfectly on my shoulders with some flare. That was, of course, then, and this is definitely now. This new incarnation of Captain Marvel is a woman, equally awesome, sans that signature cape, but decked out to be sure in some pretty nifty tights. Superhero, superheroine, no worries. The MCU is inclusive. No suspension of disbelief necessary. The buzz was that this first film – what will surely be a franchise – would be an origin story. Truth is, I have always favored the origin tales of any superhero. None has done it better than Superman in which Diane Lane and Kevin Costner play Clark’s parents and find the little guy in a capsule in a cornfield. Young Clark Kent, a kid, going to school, pushed around by bullies, and counseled by his folks to keep his powers a secret and exercise restraint. Unfortunately, the origin story for Captain Marvel has to ignore such early grand moments. Carol, the new Capt. Marvel, only acquired her powers much later. articles.text: Ongoing Elena Doronkina New Work Exhibition Returning to PCA for their second exhibition, Russian-born Elena Doronkina and Alexander Zimin have an exhibit that is open through September 22. Elena drew rave reviews in the summer of 2023 with her first exhibition here with still-lifes, figurative works, and landscapes. An award-winning artist and member of American Women Artists, she is also Program Director at the Alamo Danville Artist’s Society and manager at Blackhawk Gallery in Danville. The exhibit will be open for viewing on Saturdays and Sundays from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. The artists will host an opening reception on Saturday, September 7, from 6 to 9 p.m., during which Natalya Biktairova will show her fabric works also. articles.text: Karma Stephens Roberts, a former teacher at Piedmont Middle School, passed away on August 27, 2024, in Reston, Virginia. Born on August 2, 1949 in Portland, Oregon, Karma spent her early years in Eugene, where she cultivated her lifelong passion for education and travel. She attended Stephens College in Columbia, Missouri, and later completed her studies at the University of Oregon, where she became a proud member of the Pi Beta Phi society. Karma devoted her career to teaching as an elementary and middle school teacher, specializing in special education and reading comprehension. Her enthusiasm for education extended beyond the classroom, leading a yearbook elective that inspired creativity and teamwork in her students. Karma was known for her kindness, warm spirit, and ability to make everyone feel welcome. She had a deep love for French culture and language, and her glamorous sense of style always reflected her elegance and joie de vivre. She is predeceased by her brother, Mark, and her parents, Beulah and Wilfred Chapman. She is survived by her two children, Hilary and Mark Roberts, Karma Roberts, a former teacher at Piedmont Middle School, died on August 27, 2024. She was 75. and two adored grandchildren. A memorial service celebrating Karma’s life will be held on September 12, 2024, at 10:00 a.m. Eastern Time at the Fairfax Memorial Home in Fairfax, VA. In addition to her educational legacy, Karma’s philanthropic efforts in the Bay Area and her contributions to higher education will be fondly remembered. Her warmth, generosity, and passion for life will live on in the hearts of all who knew her.

articles.text: Jean Anderson McIntyre, 94, the mother of former Piedmont resident Claire Kostic and a longtime Atherton resident, passed away peacefully on August 28, 2024 in Palo Alto, after a short illness. She will be sorely missed. Jean will be remembered for her passion for music and music education. She was an accomplished pianist and loved Debussy, Chopin and Beethoven. She practiced at least one hour every day and filled the house with beautiful music. Jean shared her love of music through teaching piano to many children, including her own. She also loved the opera and symphony and was an active supporter of the San Francisco Symphony, San Francisco Opera, and San Francisco Ballet. Jean was born on November 20, 1929 to Niles and Olga Anderson in Everett, Washington. At age 12 her family moved to Toronto where Jean graduated from The Bishop-Strachan School. She went on to study music at Vassar College, graduating in 1951 after completing a thesis comparing personality traits to musical tastes. After graduation, Jean landed her first job in Chicago doing research on how music could help with mental illness. In 1953, Jean moved to San Diego, where her parents had retired. There, she met and married Ray Stewart. They moved to the San Francisco peninsula a year later when Ray started his career with Ampex. In 1963, Jean and Ray bought their home in Atherton, where they raised their five children. Jean was very active with her children’s education and served on the PTA of Selby Lane School and Menlo School and was a board member of Castilleja School from 1971–1982 and longtime supporter of her grandchildren’s schools in Piedmont. Jean started a legacy at Camp Four Winds on Orcas Island where all of her children either attended as well as her granddaughters. She also enjoyed gardening and was a gracious hostess to her circle of friends. In 1973, Jean married Dr. Harold Christian Zweng, who passed away in 1977. As a new widow, she became a successful real estate broker in the mid-peninsula. In 1996, she married Henry McIntyre. Throughout their marriage, Jean and Henry enjoyed extensive travel throughout the world. They loved living in their winter home in Indian Wells playing golf, bridge, and tennis and at their El Dorado Country Club, Cypress Point in Pebble Beach, Burlingame Country Club, and Menlo Circus Club. Henry passed away in 2003 and Jean never remarried but had a long-time companionship with Dr. Norman Snyder of Atherton for over ten years until he passed away in 2014. Jean loved card games, especially bridge. For those who did not share her bridge passion, she taught them to play the card game “Onze”. She also loved having her children and grandchildren over for pool gatherings, including salmon barbecues. Jean’s last 10 years included a move to the Vi in Palo Alto. She continued to enjoy traveling on many San Francisco Ballet tours all over the world with her daughter, Claire. Jean Anderson McIntyre passed away on August 28 at the age of 94. She is survived by her five children: Sandra Stewart MacPhail (Jack) of Portland, OR; Claire Stewart Kostic (Mark) of Atherton, Sharon Stewart of Ukiah, Kim Stewart of Los Altos, and David Stewart of Barcelona, Spain. She also is survived by nine grandchildren: Sheldon Stevenson (Suzanne), Jeffrey Stevenson (Erin), Creighton Stevenson, Kirsten Hanafee, Sean Hanafee, Emily Bortz, Eddie Bortz, Camila Stewart, and Giana Stewart, as well as two great-grandchildren, Finn Stevenson and Charles Stevenson. Jean is predeceased by her husband, Henry, and by her sister, Laurel Bates. A private service will be held with family and friends at the Menlo Circus Club in Atherton. In lieu of flowers, the family requests memorial donations be made in her name to San Francisco Ballet, San Francisco Opera, and San Francisco Symphony.

articles.text: Of all the AVAs in the Rhone Valley none is as historic and storied as Hermitage. Legend has it a knight returning home wounded from the Crusades in 1224 was given permission to build a small refuge to recover in on this grand hill in a bend in the Rhone River across from the town of Tain. In 1937 it was established as one of France’s first wine appellations. The vines grow on the southwest side of the steep granite hill facing the afternoon sun and are divided into a number of smaller vineyards. Syrah is the primary red grape and Marsanne and Rousanne are the white grapes. Hermitage reds tend toward being very earthy with aromas of leather, red berries, earth and coffee. They have a high level of tannins and are considered the longest lived within France. The Sorrel family’s roots in Hermitage go back to 1893 when they purchased land on the hill. Today the family’s third generation of winemakers, the three Sorrel brothers, tend the family’s few acres of land producing only a handful of bottles each vintage. Production methods are very traditional, and the wine is aged in four-year-old neutral barrels and limited to fewer than 4,000 bottles each vintage. • 2020 JMB Sorrel Hermitage Le Vignon, $75 A selection of fruit from three separate parcels: “Les Plantiers” sandy and stony, “Les Greffieux” with glacial stones and clay, and “Les Bessards,” south facing granitic soils. It shows lovely aromas of violets, leather, cured meat, blackberries and black olives. Full-bodied with a rich, velvety feel on the finish, it is bursting with life and totally enjoyable now but will age for many decades in the cellar.

articles.text: When drawing up your estate plans, you might find it useful to create a revocable or irrevocable trust, either of which can help your estate avoid probate court and give you significant control over how and when your assets are distributed. But who should oversee your trust? As the person who established the trust — known as the “grantor” or “settlor” — you can also name yourself as trustee. However, this may not be the best move, particularly if the trust is irrevocable. An irrevocable trust protects the assets in the trust from creditors and civil judgments, but if you serve as trustee, this protection will disappear. It might be more advantageous for you to be the trustee of a revocable (living) trust, which can be modified without much trouble and allows you to move assets in and out of the trust and to change trust beneficiaries. You should work with a qualified estate-planning attorney to determine which type of trust, if any, is appropriate for your situation, and to get some guidance on the wisdom of serving as your own trustee. If you decide to choose someone else as trustee, you’ll want to consider the following factors: • Trust In thinking about whom you might want to serve as your trustee, the most important attribute is trust. Do you trust that this individual will always act in your best interest? If so, then they may be a good trustee candidate, but you’ll also need to look at other considerations. • Financial management skills The person you choose to be your trustee doesn’t have to be an accountant or a financial professional — but they should be skilled at managing their own finances. And they should be well-organized and good with details. • Mental and physical fitness Your trustee could serve in that position for many years, so you’ll want to name someone who is in good physical and mental health. Of course, things can change over time, so if you observe that your chosen trustee has begun to suffer physical or mental decline, you may need to name a successor trustee in your trust document. • Conflict of interest You want your trustee to carry out your wishes in a fair manner — so, you should pick someone who doesn’t have a conflict of interest with any of the beneficiaries you’ve named in your trust. Of course, this can be tricky if you want to name a family member as trustee. So, if you do, you’ll need to spell out your wishes clearly — to the trustee and to other family members. Here’s something else to think about: Instead of choosing an individual, you could name a corporate trustee. By doing so, you can receive some key benefits, such as objectivity and potentially avoiding some of the family-related disputes that can arise when an estate is settled. Also, corporate trustees have the expertise and resources to navigate the various tax and inheritance laws affecting living trusts. Whether it’s a trusted individual or a corporate entity, the right trustee can make a big difference in the effectiveness of your living trust — and, by extension, the outcome of your comprehensive estate plans. So, start your search, get the help you need and take the steps necessary to arrive at a choice for trustee that’s right for you and your family. articles.text: It was going to be hot last Wednesday, so the Walking on Wednesdays group decided to take a shorter walk through the central part of Piedmont, and walk to the home of Hugh Craig on Craig Avenue and hear the story of Piedmont’s first mayor. He was a central figure in the City of Piedmont’s first years in the aftermath of the 1906 San Francisco earthquake when many people moved to Oakland and Piedmont. Oakland was looking for property taxes to pay for the additional services it needed to provide. It wanted to annex Piedmont, but some Piedmont residents wanted to incorporate it as a separate city. It was a race and those who favored incorporation had to move quickly. They needed a map to file incorporation papers in Sacramento, so they used a map from the Piedmont Sanitary District. This explains why some Piedmont homes are partially in Oakland. On January 7, 1907, Craig and another Piedmonter went to Sacramento to file the incorporation papers with the State. This incorporation had to be approved by the voters, and on January 26, 1907, 79 Piedmont men voted for incorporation and 38 voted against it. It was all men because women didn’t get the right to vote until 1920. On January 31, 1907, the State approved Piedmont’s incorporation. However, immediately there were problems and some Piedmonters wanted to vote again about being a separate city. On September 5, 1907 a vote on disincorporating and becoming part of Oakland was held. Approval required a 2/3 vote. Ninety-two men voted to disincorporate and 62 voted to stay a separate city. The vote to disincorporate failed by only 10 votes. For the Wednesday Walkers, it was a short stroll up Highland and Mountain Avenues to Craig’s house. He was one of the first five Piedmont settlers. He was also a San Francisco insurance man and twice president of the San Francisco Chamber of Commerce. Craig was born in Sydney, Australia in 1841 to Scottish parents. He grew up in New Zealand before moving to Oakland in 1874 to work in San Francisco for the New Zealand Insurance Company. He bought five acres and built a house in 1879 on Vernal (now Highland) Avenue. However, Highland was widened in 1912, so Craig had his home put on log rollers and pulled by horses to its current location at the corner of Craig and Mountain Avenue. Craig is known as the first Mayor of Piedmont, but there were one or two men who held the position before him. He was a central figure in the City of Piedmont’s first years in the aftermath of the 1906 San Francisco earthquake when many people moved to Oakland and Piedmont. Oakland was looking for property taxes to pay for the additional services it needed to provide. It wanted to annex Piedmont, but some Piedmont residents wanted to incorporate it as a separate city. It was a race and those who favored incorporation had to move quickly. They needed a map to file incorporation papers in Sacramento, so they used a map from the Piedmont Sanitary District. This explains why some Piedmont homes are partially in Oakland. On January 7, 1907, Craig and another Piedmonter went to Sacramento to file the incorporation papers with the State. This incorporation had to be approved by the voters, and on January 26, 1907, 79 Piedmont men voted for incorporation and 38 voted against it. It was all men because women didn’t get the right to vote until 1920. On January 31, 1907, the State approved Piedmont’s incorporation. However, immediately there were problems and some Piedmonters wanted to vote again about being a separate city. On September 5, 1907 a vote on disincorporating and becoming part of Oakland was held. Approval required a 2/3 vote. Ninety-two men voted to disincorporate and 62 voted to stay a separate city. The vote to disincorporate failed by only 10 votes.
